body:
Two moduli, one hidden relation

Purpose. Define the discrete-log problem and its two moduli before constructing the quantum function that hides the key in equal outputs.

The public points satisfy \(Q=[d]P\). The private key is the scalar \(d\in\mathbb Z_r\), where \(r\) is the order of \(P\). Coordinates instead live in \(\mathbb F_p\). Coordinate division uses an inverse modulo \(p\); key recovery uses one modulo \(r\).

\[ E:\ y^2=x^3+7\pmod p,\qquad p=2^{256}-(2^{32}+977). \]

The useful quantum function is \(f(k,l)=[k]P+[l]Q=[k+dl]P\). Here \(k\) and \(l\) are scalar labels, while \(A\) denotes the curve-point accumulator that will hold \(f(k,l)\). Equal outputs reveal a linear relation among the inputs, even though the curve coordinates hide their scalar labels.

What the three register labels mean

Purpose. Explain the physical contents of each register; a point requires two coordinate registers in this implementation.

Let \(n=\lceil\log_2 r\rceil\) and let \(m\) be the chosen scalar-register width, possibly including padding. The exact-group derivation uses labels in \(\mathbb Z_r\); the qubit circuit instead uses binary labels from \(0\) to \(2^m-1\).

LabelMathematical valueStorage in the logical arithmetic circuit
\(k,l\)Binary integers whose point multiples depend only on their residue modulo \(r\)Two \(m\)-qubit scalar registers in the clean theoretical circuit. The implementation later measures and reuses small window registers.
\(A\)One curve pointTwo field-element registers, \(A=(x_A,y_A)\), each containing 256 logical qubits. Fault-tolerant encoding stores the logical qubits collectively in larger physical code blocks. “One point register” therefore bundles two coordinate registers. This is the chosen affine representation, not an information-theoretic lower bound on storing a point.

The ideal oracle starts \(A\) at the identity \(\mathcal O\). The compiled circuit instead starts from a known random nonzero point and shifts every lookup table; this avoids identity table entries and randomizes the remaining exceptional affine-addition cases; it does not eliminate every exception. The known total shift does not change the Fourier statistics.

A line becomes a Fourier constraint

Purpose. Derive the inherited Fourier-sampling mechanism: inputs producing one point interfere to reveal a linear equation for the secret key.

Here \(F_r\lvert a\rangle=r^{-1/2}\sum_u e^{2\pi iau/r}\lvert u\rangle\). All labels in the following exact-group calculation are modulo \(r\), including both measured frequencies \(u,v\). The binary circuit below uses a different transform size.

For general order \(r\): why only one frequency line survives

Conditioning on output \([c]P\) leaves this uniform coset. Measuring the output is optional: tracing it out gives the same control statistics.

\[ |\psi_c\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_l|c-dl,l\rangle \xrightarrow{F_r^\dagger\otimes F_r^\dagger} \frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_u e^{-2\pi icu/r}|u,du\rangle. \]

The amplitude at \((u,v)\) contains \(\sum_l e^{2\pi il(du-v)/r}\): a geometric sum equal to \(r\) when \(v=du\), otherwise zero. The unknown offset \(c\) changes only phases.

Qubits broaden the peaks

Purpose. Explain a practical limitation, not a new speedup: binary-sized registers broaden the ideal peaks and require a separate success bound.

Actual controls have size \(M=2^m\), not \(r\). Their finite input lines produce broadened Fourier peaks; the exact-group success \(1-1/r\) no longer applies. Equivalently, the commuting translations by \(P,Q\) perform two phase estimates with a shared uniform eigenlabel \(s\):

\[ \theta_1=s/r,\qquad \theta_2=(ds\bmod r)/r. \]

Sufficient precision lets rounding recover both numerators. Mosca's bound controls those samples; Ekerå's search can recover additional ones.

First do the computation classically

Purpose. Reduce expensive point additions by classically precomputing the contribution of each group of scalar bits.

Given the public points \(P,Q\), the task is to evaluate \([k]P+[l]Q\). Temporarily treat \(k,l\) as ordinary integers. Split each into groups of \(w\) bits:

\[k=\sum_i k_i2^{iw},\qquad l=\sum_i l_i2^{iw},\qquad 0\le k_i,l_i<2^w.\]

Window position \(i\) is fixed by the schedule; window value \(k_i\) is the address. Before running the quantum computer, use ordinary curve arithmetic to compute

\[T_i^{(P)}[j]=[j2^{iw}]P,\qquad T_i^{(Q)}[j]=[j2^{iw}]Q.\]

These are tables of known coordinate pairs. Constructing the Q tables needs the public point Q, not its unknown discrete logarithm d. With \(w=2\), the P tables begin:

Address jWindow 0: T₀[j]Window 1: T₁[j]
0\(\mathcal O\)\(\mathcal O\)
1\(P\)\([4]P\)
2\([2]P\)\([8]P\)
3\([3]P\)\([12]P\)

Start an accumulator A, then update \(A\leftarrow A+T_i[k_i]\) once per window. For \(k=11=3+4\cdot2\), select row 3 of table 0 and row 2 of table 1: \(\mathcal O\to[3]P\to[11]P\). Repeat with the Q tables and l to obtain \([k]P+[l]Q\). The implemented tables have \(2^{16}=65{,}536\) entries each.

The identity entries above illustrate the unshifted mathematical tables. In the paper, choose a known offset \(R_i\) for each table so that \(T_i[j]=[j2^{iw}]P+R_i\ne\mathcal O\), and start from a known nonzero point \(A_0\). The final point gains the constant \(A_0+\sum_iR_i\), including both sets of windows. This translation leaves the Fourier statistics unchanged. Other exceptional affine additions still require the paper’s failure analysis.

What one accumulator update computes

Purpose. Identify the modular division, multiplication and squaring that make each point addition expensive.

A is one point with two coordinates, \(A=(x_1,y_1)\); the selected entry is \(T_i[j]=(x_2,y_2)\). For a nonexceptional addition, first find the slope, then the new coordinates, all modulo p:

\[\lambda=(y_1-y_2)(x_1-x_2)^{-1},\qquad x_3=\lambda^2-x_1-x_2,\qquad y_3=\lambda(x_2-x_3)-y_2.\]

Division is a modular inverse followed by multiplication. This is why a gcd circuit appears: extended Euclid finds \(a\Delta x+bp=1\), making a the inverse of Δx modulo p. The paper applies that inverse through recorded binary-gcd steps. Why the gcd computes the required division. These formulas explain the division, squaring and multiplication circuits in Section V. A classical program may overwrite temporary values freely; a quantum circuit must also clear workspace without revealing which address was selected.

Now make the lookup coherent

Purpose. Implement table selection coherently; the precomputed entries become gates, while only the selected word occupies the output register.

The table entries stay classical constants, compiled into the gate sequence. The address j becomes a w-qubit register. Let \(F_i(j)\) concatenate the coordinate bits of \(T_i[j]\). The reversible lookup is the XOR operation

\[L_i:|j\rangle|z\rangle\longmapsto |j\rangle|z\oplus F_i(j)\rangle.\]

Bitwise XOR is not elliptic-curve addition. Starting z at zero loads the coordinate bits; applying the same lookup again clears them. Linearity gives

\[\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|0\rangle\longmapsto\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|F_i(j)\rangle.\]

No classical processor reads j during this operation. It may entangle the address with the output while preserving their coherence.

Inside the lookup: a complete two-bit example

Purpose. Show exactly how address-controlled bit flips implement a small table, before introducing the more efficient traversal.

To see every gate, temporarily replace the 512-bit coordinate word with a two-bit word \(f_1f_0\). This is a toy data table, not a toy elliptic curve:

Address j₁j₀Stored word f₁f₀Output bits to flip
0001z₀
0110z₁
1011z₁ and z₀
1100None

For input 10, only the last two gates fire, producing 11. For a superposition, each basis address follows its own row without being measured. For arbitrary initial output z, this circuit computes \(z\oplus f(j)\), so it is reversible on all inputs.

How this scales to a long coordinate word

Purpose. Avoid testing the same address independently for every coordinate bit by reusing a selector.

Testing the same address separately for every output bit repeats work. Instead, compute a selector \(a=[j=t]\) once for a fixed row t, use it to flip all the row’s 1 bits, then erase it:

The paper uses an optimized unary lookup: successive row selectors share partial address tests. Its compiler further overlaps two traversals (“zipper” lookup). These optimizations change cost and scheduling, while preserving the XOR map above. The drawing is a unitary compute–copy–uncompute explanation; the implementation can replace parts of cleanup with measurements and phase corrections.

The shared-test circuit behind unary lookup

Purpose. Reduce nonlinear work by sharing one AND computation between the two branches of a lookup.

In the circuit below, c enables a subtree, x is its next address bit, and D₀,D₁ are fixed output words. Compute a=cx once, load D₁ under that control, change a to c(1−x) with a CNOT, then load D₀. Restore a and erase it by X measurement plus a conditional CZ. Thus one AND serves an entire output word.

Continue through the full circuit sequence → Expand this into an eight-entry LUT, then the paper’s two controlled 15-bit zipper traversals, block relays, and coordinate-output phase repair.

Use the loaded point, then clear it

Purpose. Combine lookup and point addition while restoring temporary storage; the optimized schedule later trades extra lookups for fewer live qubits.

The following register circuit combines the lookup with an accumulator update. A and work each bundle two coordinate registers. It shows the simple logical construction, before the paper’s workspace optimizations.

Why the paper has three lookups per addition: it releases table outputs early to reuse their space. The first loads \((x_2,y_2)\) to form differences; the second loads \(3x_2\) for the square-subtract stage; the third reloads coordinates to remove the final offsets. X-basis cleanup frees the outputs but produces address-dependent phases, repaired by a phase-fix lookup. Thus three forward lookups serve one point addition, not three different windows. See the measurement, reset and feedforward cleanup circuit.

ChangeWhat it savesWhat it costs
16-bit windowsOne addition per window\(2^{16}\)-entry lookups
Direct first lookupThe first additionA separately charged initialization
Omit three windowsThree more additions; 28 remainClassical recovery of 48 missing bits
Measure and reuse controlsTwo persistent scalar registersAdaptive Fourier rotations and feedforward

The conservative branch adds a control bit per scalar, enlarging the initial lookup to \(2^{18}\) entries. Subsequent windows remain 16 bits. The accumulator stays coherent while this small control window is reused.

title: III. From an elliptic-curve key to a Fourier sample

body:
The headline combines different claims

Purpose. Separate the probability claims that are multiplied or bounded to obtain an end-to-end success estimate.

The task is to recover \(d\) from \(Q=[d]P\) in a known prime-order group of order \(r\). The oracle evaluates \([k]P+[l]Q\) coherently; \(k,l\) label its two scalar inputs. Here \(L\) is total modeled hardware-failure probability, not a window count.

Ideal recovery

\(P_0\): Fourier sampling plus classical search.

Approximate arithmetic

\(p_f\): bad values or phases under fresh randomness.

Physical execution

\(1-L\): no logical fault in the hardware model.

The \(1-2^{-128}\) confidence statement concerns sampling used to bound arithmetic failure. It does not certify the device or mean an attempt succeeds with that probability.

Wrong phases count as wrong answers

Purpose. Count relative-phase errors as oracle failures even when the computed coordinates look correct.

In the cleanup formula, \(b(x)\) is the computed work bit and \(m\) its X-readout bit. Both take values in \(\{0,1\}\). \(B_\omega\) contains labels with wrong outputs or relative phases at fixed randomness \(\omega\).

For every fixed control label \(x=(k,l)\), let \(B_\omega\) contain wrong outputs and residual minus signs. The randomness \(\omega\) includes masks and \(X\)-basis cleanup outcomes:

\[ \forall x:\quad\Pr_\omega(x\in B_\omega)\le p_f. \]

A cleanup readout contributes \(2^{-1/2}(-1)^{mb(x)}\): its magnitude is input-independent, so each readout is uniform even conditioned on earlier ones. Its sign can still spoil interference.

The values may look right while the Fourier answer changes: \(|+\rangle\xrightarrow{Z}|-\rangle\), then \(H|+\rangle=|0\rangle\) but \(H|-\rangle=|1\rangle\).

Known final point translations can be undone hypothetically: they permute only the output register and preserve control statistics. This aligns every ideal seed with one state \(|\Psi\rangle\).

Randomization gives a linear amplitude penalty

Purpose. Use random masks to bound the damage from bad inputs at the amplitude level.

\(\widetilde P\) is averaged approximate-oracle recovery probability; \(P_0\) is the exact-oracle baseline. Norms are Hilbert-space vector norms. Include all uncleared work in the output when identifying bad branches.

\[ \boxed{\widetilde P\ge\bigl(\max\{0,\sqrt{P_0}-2p_f\}\bigr)^2.} \]

The penalty is \(2p_f\), not \(2\sqrt{p_f}\). The pointwise guarantee lets us average each label's error before taking its norm.

Proof: average, bound, project

For \(N\) uniform input labels, write the mean error \(\Delta=\mathbb E_\omega|\widetilde\Psi_\omega\rangle-|\Psi\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_x|x\rangle|d_x\rangle\). On a good label the error is zero; on a bad one it is the difference of two unit vectors. Thus

\[ \|d_x\|\le2\Pr_\omega(x\in B_\omega)\le2p_f, \qquad \|\Delta\|^2=\frac1N\sum_x\|d_x\|^2\le4p_f^2. \]

For the seed-independent success projector \(M\), Jensen's inequality and the reverse triangle inequality give

\[ \mathbb E_\omega\|M\widetilde\Psi_\omega\|^2 \ge\|M\mathbb E_\omega\widetilde\Psi_\omega\|^2 \ge\bigl(\max\{0,\sqrt{P_0}-\|\Delta\|\}\bigr)^2. \]

The mean ket is a proof device, not the physical mixed state. The first expression is the actual averaged probability.

A tight example. Flip one uniformly chosen sign in an \(N\)-term uniform state. Each label is bad with probability \(1/N\); projection back onto the uniform state succeeds with \((1-2/N)^2\).

Two routes to the reported probabilities

Purpose. Assemble the conservative and heuristic success estimates with their different recovery assumptions.

Appendix B gives \(p_f\le0.03346\); the main calculation rounds upward to \(0.0335\).

Ideal baselineAfter arithmeticAfter modeled hardware
Mosca: \(0.6570\)\((\sqrt{0.6570}-0.067)^2\approx0.553\)\(0.553\times0.7355\approx40.7\%\)
Ekerå heuristic: \(0.99\)\((\sqrt{0.99}-0.067)^2\approx0.861\)\(0.861\times0.7355\approx63.3\%\)

Mosca's theorem assumes sufficient phase resolution. Applying it after omitting 48 bits requires classical search covering the missing ambiguity. Ekerå's 99% branch is heuristic; propagating it through an inequality does not make it rigorous. Hardware multiplication assumes the no-logical-fault branch follows the stated algorithmic distribution.

What one attempt buys

Purpose. Explain how independent repetitions change the chance of recovering a valid key.

Verify a candidate by checking \([d]P=Q\). Independent attempts with success \(s\) give \(1-(1-s)^m\) after \(m\) tries. The 25.7-day estimate times one quantum attempt; the paper does not supply full classical search cutoffs and a runtime benchmark for recovering the omitted 48 bits.

summary: The paper bounds how deliberate arithmetic errors reduce Fourier-sampling success, then combines that with classical recovery and modeled hardware survival. Its randomization argument strengthens the analysis; the heuristic and conservative recovery branches remain distinct.
title: IV. What does a 63% success probability mean?

body:
Approximation is paid for in success probability

Purpose. Identify all deliberate approximation mechanisms before assigning a total failure probability.

Here \(p=2^n-c\) is the coordinate-field prime, \(n=256\), \(c=2^{32}+977\), and \(r\) is the curve-group order. A scalar window has \(w=16\) bits. Canonical field values are integers from \(0\) to \(p-1\); \(\mathcal O\) is the group identity.

Appendix B counts failures of an otherwise noiseless logical circuit. Bad values, noncanonical outputs, residual phases and uncleared ancillas all matter. The guarantee is for every fixed scalar input, averaged over fresh masks and uniform \(X\)-basis cleanup readouts.

Randomize

Move a fixed input through the arithmetic's bad sets.

Count

Bound each possible first failure along the ideal path.

Transfer

Turn those counts into a Fourier-success bound.

Reversibility adds an exceptional point

Purpose. Include exceptional inputs created by reversible cleanup as well as ordinary affine point addition.

Adding a fixed point \(C\) is a permutation. Its chosen affine formula is incomplete:

OperationDivision usedExceptional input \(A\)
Compute slope\((y_A-y_C)/(x_A-x_C)\)\(C,-C\), or nonaffine \(\mathcal O\)
Erase slope from output\((y_C+y_{A+C})/(x_C-x_{A+C})\)\(\mathcal O,-2C\)

The easily missed case is \(A=-2C\): the forward sum exists, but its output \(-C\) has the same \(x\)-coordinate as \(C\), preventing slope cleanup.

A uniform nonidentity accumulator offset and random table shifts spread these cases. For a fixed window and digit, varying the offset makes the selected entry uniform over \(r-2^w\) allowed points; a fixed table itself is deterministic. Before the first failure, \(\mathcal O\) was already excluded by an earlier opposite-point addition. Only three newly bad offsets remain per step:

\[ p_{\rm exception}\le\frac{6L}{r-1},\qquad L=\lceil n/w\rceil=16. \]

Short carries can lose values

Purpose. Bound when shortening modular-reduction arithmetic changes the computed value.

\(\kappa,\delta,\rho\) count low correction bits, high comparison bits, and carry-padding bits. The quotient \(q_u\), remainder \(r_u\), and escape bit \(w_u\) belong to the integer \(u\); \(r_u\) is not the group order.

For \(p=2^n-c\), overflow folds back as \(2^n\equiv c\pmod p\). For \(0\le u<2^{n+1}\), write \(u=q_u2^n+r_u\), with \(q_u\in\{0,1\}\) and \(0\le r_u<2^n\). Assume \(2c\le2^\kappa\le2^n\). A correction limited to \(\kappa\) bits computes

\[ \operatorname{red}_\kappa(u)=r_u+q_uc-q_uw_u2^\kappa, \quad w_u=1[(r_u\bmod2^\kappa)\ge2^\kappa-c]. \]
BoundaryFailure mechanism
\(p\le u<2^n\)No overflow: the result stays noncanonical.
\(q_u=w_u=1\)The correction carry escapes: the result loses \(2^\kappa\).

Short comparisons can lose phases

Purpose. Bound when shortening a cleanup comparison leaves an incorrect relative phase.

Measuring an ancilla \(b(x)\) in \(X\) gives phase \((-1)^{mb(x)}\). Repair using a cheaper predicate \(\widetilde b\) leaves

\[ (-1)^{m(b(x)\oplus\widetilde b(x))}. \]

Disagreement can spoil Fourier interference even when the numeric output is correct. Charging every disagreement is conservative.

Transfer field counts to curve probabilities

Purpose. Convert field-element failure counts into probabilities for points drawn from the elliptic curve.

Let \(D=(r-1)(r-2^w)\). Counting missed reductions, escaped carries and comparison disagreements gives \(N_{\rm add}\) bad canonical field pairs. Coordinate multiplicities then transfer this count to the masked curve inputs.

The addition count and its factor 10 \[ N_{\rm add}\le 2^{n-1}c\left(1+\frac{p-2c-1}{2^\kappa}\right) +\frac{(2^{n-\delta}-1)(p-c)}2. \]

The three masked additions have at most \(4p,2(r-1),4p\) preimages per field pair. Divide their sum by \(pD\). Since \(r-1

Subtraction reuses addition through \(C(v)=p-1-v\): \(C(C(v)+u\bmod p)=v-u\bmod p\). A short complement fails on \(N_{\rm cmpl}=c(2^{n-\kappa}-1)\) inputs. Four coordinate-pair multiplicities sum to \(4+9+9+4=26\), giving

\[ p_{\rm sub}\le\frac{26N_{\rm sub}}D \le\frac{26(N_{\rm add}+2pN_{\rm cmpl})}D <1.05938\times10^{-8}. \]

Negation computes \(p-u\) and then swaps encodings \(0,p\). At \(\kappa=65\) and zero-test width \(\tau=32\), its shortened carry and zero test contribute \(p_{\rm neg}<6.9850\times10^{-10}\). At \(\kappa=65,\delta=32\), the additions contribute \(p_{\rm add}<1.74623\times10^{-9}\).

A mask makes a carry count useful

Purpose. Randomize the square-subtract input so carry-failure counts apply to the actual computation.

Adding a uniform field mask to the target of \(y\leftarrow y-x^2\) makes that target uniform for every fixed \(x\); subtracting the mask afterward restores the operation.

Failure siteConstraint on a uniform targetCount in the square
Local carryCross all \(\rho\) padding bits\(16\cdot2^{-\rho}\)
Wrapping correctionOverflow the \(\kappa\)-bit correction\((9+2\cdot13)c2^{-\kappa}\)
Phase repairEqual high \(\delta\) bits, or noncanonical target\(9\cdot2^{-\delta}+9c2^{-256}\)
\[ p_{\rm sq}\le(1+c/p)\left(16\,2^{-\rho}+35c\,2^{-\kappa} +9\,2^{-\delta}+9c\,2^{-256}\right)<9.89531\times10^{-9}. \]

Here \(\rho=\delta=32,\kappa=65\). Integer squaring and its built-and-unbuilt correction register are exact; target updates and phase cleanup cause these failures.

The dominant term is measured, then bounded

Purpose. Use sampled gcd failures with a confidence bound instead of treating observed failure frequency as exact.

Here \(q_{\rm div},q_{\rm mul}\) are true failure probabilities for the stated uniform field inputs; \(q_U\) is their statistical upper bound. \(K\) counts failures in one million independent samples. Curve inputs require the subsequent multiplicity bound.

Binary-gcd multiplication and division use shorter schedules and shrinking registers. Each simulation found 21 failures among one million uniform \((u,v)\in\mathbb F_p^*\times\mathbb F_p\) inputs.

Observed rate\[21/10^6=0.000021\]
One-sided upper bound\[q_U=0.000149304\]
Curve-input transfer\[p_{\rm gcd}\lesssim4(q_{\rm div}+q_{\rm mul})\]

The Clopper–Pearson upper bound solves \(\Pr_{q_U}[K\le21]=2^{-129}\); combining both operations gives confidence at least \(1-2^{-128}\). Reproduction must include output, phase and ancilla failures and the exact schedule's integer rounding.

Why the factor is approximately four

For fixed coordinate differences \(u\ne0,v\), subtracting the curve equations gives \(2vy+v^2=3ux^2+3u^2x+u^3\). If \(v\ne0\), substitution leaves

\[ (3ux^2+3u^2x+u^3-v^2)^2-4v^2(x^3+7)=0. \]

This quartic has at most four roots; each fixes the point. At \(v=0\), at most two \(x\)'s each admit two \(y\)'s. The inverse slope operation has the same bound. Thus

\[ p_{\rm gcd,div}+p_{\rm gcd,mul} \le\frac{4p(p-1)}D(q_{\rm div}+q_{\rm mul}). \]

Count first failures; no independence is needed

Purpose. Combine first-failure events without assuming that the different arithmetic errors are independent.

Follow the ideal computation until its first failure. A union bound over those sites gives \(p_{\rm ecadd}\le0.001195\). Nearly all of it is the transferred gcd bound: approximately \(8q_U=0.001194432\); the small arithmetic terms total about \(2.29\times10^{-8}\).

\[ p_f\le28p_{\rm ecadd}+\frac{6L}{r-1}\le0.03346. \]

The pointwise randomized guarantee then gives \(\widetilde P\ge(\max\{0,\sqrt{P_0}-2p_f\})^2\). The proof averages masks and cleanup readouts; physical faults enter separately.
summary: This appendix justifies the error budget for cheaper approximate arithmetic. It bounds exceptional inputs, lost carries and phase errors, and combines them with sampled gcd failures. The purpose is to support a success guarantee, not to make every arithmetic branch exact.
title: Appendix B. Every way the arithmetic can fail

body:
The algorithmic structure IonQ inherits

Purpose. Locate the original algorithmic contribution before discussing the later arithmetic optimizations.

Fix a known generator \(P\) of prime order \(r\) and a public point \(Q=[d]P\); \(d\in\mathbb Z_r\) is unknown. Coordinates are computed modulo the field prime \(p\). Brackets \([a]P\) denote repeated group addition, not coordinate multiplication.

Shor supplies quantum discrete-logarithm recovery. Proos and Zalka specialize the group oracle to elliptic curves over prime fields and study reversible finite-field arithmetic. IonQ retains that structure while changing the arithmetic, compiler and fault-tolerant architecture.

A cyclic group is abstractly \(\mathbb Z_r\), but the map \([a]P\mapsto a\) is exactly what is hidden. Coordinate arithmetic modulo \(p\) does not expose scalar labels modulo \(r\).

The secret is a direction, not an output

Purpose. Show how equal point outputs encode the secret direction that Fourier sampling reveals.

\[ f(k,l)=[k]P+[l]Q, \quad f(k+r,l)=f(k,l),\quad f(k+d,l-1)=f(k,l). \]

Equal-output labels form shifted copies of \(H=\{(-dl,l)\}\) over \(\mathbb Z_r^2\). The point register cannot distinguish labels within one copy, so they remain coherent.

Input direction\[(-d,1)\]
Surviving frequency\[(u,v)\cdot(-d,1)=0\]
Recovered scalar\[d=vu^{-1}\pmod r\]

The phase sum \(\sum_l e^{2\pi i(v-du)l/r}\) vanishes unless \(v=du\). For prime \(r\), any nonzero \(u\) is invertible. Binary Fourier transforms broaden this exact-group constraint into peaks.

Measuring the inputs immediately after the oracle only returns random labels. The answer lies in their interference. Leaving temporary garbage \(g(k,l)\) can distinguish labels with equal point outputs and destroy that interference; correct classical values alone do not validate the oracle.

A permutation needs clean temporary space

Purpose. Build a clean reversible translation so temporary data cannot destroy the interference needed by the algorithm.

Translation \(F_T(A)=A+T\) has inverse \(F_{-T}\). This gives a generic in-place construction:

\[ |A,0\rangle\longmapsto|A,F_T(A)\rangle \longmapsto|F_T(A),A\rangle \longmapsto|F_T(A),0\rangle. \]

The optimized circuit uses affine algebra to reduce temporary space. Cleaning its slope requires reconstructing it from the output, whose denominator can vanish when the forward one does not. This is why \(A=-2T\) joins the usual exceptional cases: the output is \(-T\), sharing \(T\)'s \(x\)-coordinate.

Reversible inversion creates the scheduling problem

Purpose. Explain why reversible inversion requires a common schedule and stored branch information in superposition.

\[ au+bp=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u^{-1}=a\pmod p. \]

Euclid's algorithm finds these coefficients. In superposition, different denominators terminate at different iterations. A common schedule and reversible branch records prevent a stopping measurement from revealing the denominator.

ChoiceConsequence
Schedule for the worst inputAll branches fit; larger circuit.
Short schedule and shrinking registersLower resources; rare branches fail.
Fresh arithmetic masksSpread those failures over fixed logical inputs.

IonQ takes the latter route and includes its failures in a sampled bound. Proos–Zalka supplies the reversible-arithmetic setting, not the new resource totals.

Classical verification is exact: a recovered \(d\) is accepted only if \([d]P=Q\). This detects unsuccessful attempts but does not increase the probability of producing a useful Fourier sample.

summary: This inherited construction solves a discrete logarithm by Fourier sampling over a cyclic group. The elliptic-curve implementation supplies reversible point arithmetic; IonQ improves that implementation and its physical realization rather than replacing the hidden-subgroup algorithm.
title: Reference [3, 24]. Why Shor works for elliptic curves

body:
Measure early, preserve the distribution

Purpose. State which output distribution is preserved when Fourier-transform qubits are measured early.

Use \(F_N\lvert y\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ixy/N}\lvert x\rangle\). The circuit measures after \(F_N^\dagger\). An X-basis measurement is Hadamard followed by Z readout. \(V\) below is any target unitary.

Griffiths and Niu replace a Fourier transform followed by measurement with adaptive single-qubit measurements. Earlier outcomes choose later phase rotations. The distribution is unchanged, including for entangled inputs. This replacement applies when the Fourier outputs are to be measured.

The whole argument is one measurement identity

Purpose. Prove the measurement identity that permits replacing a quantum control by its classical outcome.

\[ C(V)=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes V, \qquad (\langle m|\otimes I)C(V)=V^m(\langle m|\otimes I). \]

Measuring the control after a controlled gate has the same measurement operator as measuring first and applying \(V\) when the classical result is one. Since this is an operator identity, untouched entangled registers require no separate assumption.

Quantum controls become classical wires

Purpose. Translate the identity into a circuit with adaptive rotations and classical control wires.

Define \(R_j=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{2\pi i/2^j})\). Controlled phase is symmetric between its wires: the first measured wire can serve as control. Commute its measurement through the remaining phases and repeat.

A visual check: decode five

Purpose. Check the order of measured bits and corrections on one small phase-estimation example.

In \(F_8|5\rangle\), the three input wires have the relative phases below. Feedback removes the fractional phase contributed by earlier measured bits.

WireInitial phaseFeedback factorAfter feedbackBit after \(H\)
\(q_2\)\(-1\)\(1\)\(-1\)\(y_0=1\)
\(q_1\)\(i\)\(e^{-\pi i/2}\)\(+1\)\(y_1=0\)
\(q_0\)\(e^{5\pi i/4}\)\(e^{-\pi i/4}\)\(-1\)\(y_2=1\)

Thus \(y=y_0+2y_1+4y_2=5\). Output labels absorb the usual bit reversal.

Cancel the known tail

Purpose. Choose each rotation to cancel the phase contribution already revealed by earlier outcomes.

For \(y=\sum_{h=0}^{m-1}2^hy_h\), step \(j\) reads bit \(y_j\) from least to most significant. The control carries phase \(y/2^{j+1}\) modulo one. Earlier bits \(y_0,\ldots,y_{j-1}\) determine a correction angle

\[ \phi_j=-2\pi\sum_{hAfter cancellation, the relative phase is \((-1)^{y_j}\); \(H\) reveals that bit. Nonbinary eigenphases give probabilistic outcomes, still exactly matching the coherent Fourier measurement.

Reuse the controls, retain the accumulator

Purpose. Use early measurement to reuse scalar-control qubits while keeping the curve accumulator coherent.

For \(U|\psi\rangle=e^{2\pi i\theta}|\psi\rangle\), one controlled power gives

\[ |+\rangle|\psi\rangle\xrightarrow{C(U^{2^j})} \frac{|0\rangle+e^{2\pi i2^j\theta}|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}|\psi\rangle. \]

Interleave this preparation with adaptive measurement, then reset the measured control. For a superposition of eigenstates, the work-register updates agree with full phase estimation. IonQ keeps a 16-bit window to support table lookups, measures it, and reuses it; the curve accumulator remains coherent.

The memory saving leaves a timing cost: classical feedforward and accurately synthesized rotations. The compiled measurement-layer schedule charges this Fourier work.

summary: This inherited identity replaces quantum-controlled Fourier rotations with measurement and classical feedforward. It preserves the final measurement distribution while allowing control qubits to be measured and reused, at the cost of adaptive timing.
title: Reference [57]. Measuring the Fourier transform one qubit at a time

body:
Why the conservative baseline is 65.7%

Purpose. Identify the rigorous ideal-algorithm baseline before arithmetic and hardware errors are included.

Fix a generator \(P\) of known prime order \(r\), with \(Q=[d]P\). The secret is \(d\in\mathbb Z_r\); the sampled eigenlabel is \(s\in\mathbb Z_r\). This lesson first assumes exact group arithmetic and full phase-estimation precision; shortened controls are discussed last.

Mosca's Corollary 19 gives a recovery bound for a known prime-order group and sufficiently precise binary phase estimation. IonQ imports the bound

\[ P_0\ge\frac{r-1}{r}\left(\frac8{\pi^2}\right)^2\approx0.6570. \]

The two factors come from two phase estimates sharing one hidden eigenlabel.

Two measurements of the same hidden label

Purpose. Explain why the two phase estimates share one underlying group eigenlabel.

\[ |\chi_s\rangle=\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_a e^{-2\pi isa/r}|[a]P\rangle, \quad \theta_1=s/r,\quad\theta_2=(ds\bmod r)/r. \]

The eigenvector sum runs over \(a=0,\ldots,r-1\); \(\theta_1,\theta_2\) are phases in turns, not radians. Translations by \(P,Q\) share these eigenvectors. The identity point is a uniform superposition over \(s\). Conditional on \(s\), the phase-estimation distributions factor; the two numerators themselves are related, not independent.

Bound a peak, then convert it to an integer

Purpose. Bound the probability of a useful Fourier outcome close enough to recover the desired integer.

For \(M=2^m\) control states, the geometric sum gives

\[ \Pr(z\mid\theta)=\left|\frac1M\sum_{a=0}^{M-1}e^{2\pi ia(\theta-z/M)}\right|^2 =\frac{\sin^2(\pi M(\theta-z/M))}{M^2\sin^2(\pi(\theta-z/M))}. \]

At an exactly representable phase the corresponding outcome is certain. Otherwise write \(M\theta=j+\alpha\), \(0<\alpha<1\).

Left neighbor\[z=j,\quad\text{error}=\alpha/M\]
Hidden phase\[M\theta=j+\alpha\]
Right neighbor\[z=j+1,\quad\text{error}=(1-\alpha)/M\]

Using \(|\sin t|\le|t|\) in the denominators yields

\[ \Pr(j)+\Pr(j+1)\ge \frac{\sin^2(\pi\alpha)}{\pi^2}\left(\frac1{\alpha^2}+\frac1{(1-\alpha)^2}\right) \ge\frac8{\pi^2}. \]

The symmetric expression is minimized at \(\alpha=1/2\). Both neighbors count; bounding only the closest gives the weaker \(4/\pi^2\).

One extra bit makes both neighbors useful

Purpose. Show how one extra precision bit makes both neighboring Fourier outcomes useful for rounding.

\[ M\ge2r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |z/M-s/r|<1/M\le1/(2r) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{round}(rz/M)=s. \]

Distances are circular and the recovered numerator is modulo \(r\). If \(r\) has \(n\) bits, \(M=2^{n+1}\) suffices. Mosca presents two padding bits; IonQ notes that this argument needs only one.

One check. For \(r=19,M=64,s=3\), the two neighboring outcomes 10 and 11 both satisfy \(\operatorname{round}(19z/64)=3\).

Both phase estimates meet their rounding conditions with probability at least \((8/\pi^2)^2\). The uniform eigenlabel is nonzero with probability \((r-1)/r\); then \(d=(ds\bmod r)s^{-1}\). Multiplying these guarantees gives the stated baseline.

The omitted 48 bits need an additional argument

Purpose. Identify the gap between the full-precision bound and the implementation that omits scalar windows.

The theorem assumes an exact oracle and the stated resolution. IonQ also shortens phase estimation by 48 bits. Nearest rounding alone does not cover that configuration: classical search must recover the missing ambiguity. A full reproduction must specify its cutoffs and successful-sample set. Ekerå's lesson separates the exact recovery equation from the heuristic probability analysis.

Arithmetic failures and physical logical faults enter afterward. Neither this theorem nor its arithmetic adjustment certifies the end-to-end hardware prediction.

refs.role: Verified primary theorem and phase-accuracy requirement
refs.title: Mosca, Quantum Computer Algorithms (1999), Corollary 19

summary: This inherited Fourier bound supplies the conservative ideal-success baseline. The lesson explains the precision needed to recover two phase numerators; the shortened-register implementation still needs an additional classical-recovery assumption.
title: Reference [56]. Deriving the conservative Fourier success bound

body:
Missing quantum bits become classical search

Purpose. Explain the quantum work saved by accepting less precise samples and doing more classical recovery.

The public input is \(P,Q=[d]P\) in a known prime-order group of order \(r\). Scalars are reduced modulo \(r\), while the register lengths \(A,B\) below are powers of two. These \(A,B\) are dimensions, not curve points.

Ekerå studies binary Fourier sampling with shorter controls and searches around its peaks. IonQ omits three 16-bit windows and takes a heuristic 99% ideal-success baseline. The recovery equation is exact; the probability that a practical search succeeds is a separate claim.

Fix the sign and register lengths

Purpose. Define the phase samples and sign convention before writing the recovery equation.

\[ A=2^{m+\varsigma},\quad B=2^\ell,\qquad (a,b)\longmapsto[a]P-[b]Q, \quad0\le aHere \(m\) is the bitlength of \(r\), \(\varsigma\) is padding, and \(\ell\) tunes the second control. Use positive-exponent Fourier transforms with outcomes \((j,k)\). This minus-oracle convention requires negating the corresponding Fourier label when translating from IonQ's plus-oracle.

A useful sample has two small corrections

Purpose. Express imperfect samples using small integer corrections that classical search can recover.

Round the sample\[z=\operatorname{round}(rj/A),\quad C=\operatorname{round}(rk/B)\]
Search nearby relations\[d(z+\eta)+C=t\pmod r\]
Recover and verify\[d=(t-C)(z+\eta)^{-1}\pmod r\]

Try the chosen intervals for peak-branch offset \(\eta\) and residual \(t\); skip noninvertible \(z+\eta\). Accept a candidate only when \([d]P=Q\).

A sample rescued by one correction. Modulo 19, let \(z=3,C=16\). The zero-offset candidate is 1. Trying \(t=-1,\eta=0\) instead gives \((-1-16)3^{-1}=7\). This checks the recovery algebra, not that sample's probability.
Where the integer relation comes from

For a relevant peak with integer displacement \(\Delta\) and rounding offset \(\delta_\eta\in[-1/2,1/2)\), with \(n_d\) an integer accounting for modular wrapping, the phase relation has the form

\[ d(z+\eta)+rk/B+n_dr=r(\Delta-\delta_\eta)/B. \]

Round both sides. Integer terms pass through rounding, yielding \(d(z+\eta)+C+n_dr=t\), where \(t=\operatorname{round}(r(\Delta-\delta_\eta)/B)\). Reduce modulo \(r\).

Why 99% is heuristic

Purpose. Identify the distributional assumption behind the high quoted recovery probability.

For angular displacement \(\phi\) from a peak, in radians, a length-\(B\) control produces the profile

\[ h(\phi)=\frac1{B^2}\left|\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}e^{ib\phi}\right|^2 =\frac{\sin^2(B\phi/2)}{B^2\sin^2(\phi/2)}. \]

Its width is of order \(1/B\). Ekerå approximates distinct peak families as contributing separately when \(d/r\) lacks unusually good small-denominator rational approximations. The exact distribution also contains interference between families. Numerical integration under this approximation estimates how much probability the chosen search captures.

A known shift \(Q\mapsto Q+[a]P\) can randomize \(d\), then be undone after recovery. This distribution argument is distinct from arithmetic-failure masks.

The tradeoff has a square-root search cost

Purpose. Quantify the search cost paid when quantum precision is reduced.

\[ |t|\lesssim \frac r{2^\ell}(B_\Delta+1/2), \qquad [t]P=[C]P+[z+\eta]Q. \]

Here \(B_\Delta\) bounds accepted peak displacement. Removing one control bit roughly doubles the residual interval, at fixed other parameters. For each \(\eta\), the group equation is a discrete logarithm in that interval.

Residual intervalDirect candidate searchMeet-in-the-middle scale
\(W\) integers\(W\) trials\(\sqrt W\) stored points and operations
Illustration: \(W=2^{48}\)\(2^{48}\)\(2^{24}\), before constants and peak factors

Split \(t=a+sb\), \(s\approx\sqrt W\); define \(Q'_\eta=[C]P+[z+\eta]Q\), and match stored \([a]P\) against \(Q'_\eta-[sb]P\). These \(a,b\) are classical search indices. This explains the scaling without promising a timed implementation.

What the headline leaves unspecified

Purpose. State which recovery parameters and implementation details are needed to reproduce the quoted performance.

IonQ does not supply all search cutoffs, time-memory settings and a classical runtime benchmark for its omitted 48 bits. Its 63.3% end-to-end estimate retains the heuristic recovery assumption. Ekerå's known-logarithm simulator can test distribution predictions; it cannot solve an unknown logarithm by itself.

summary: This inherited classical recovery method trades quantum precision for a larger classical search. It helps justify omitting costly windows, but the high success estimate uses a heuristic distribution and must be distinguished from the conservative bound.
title: Reference [37]. Trading phase-estimation work for classical search
